statement: The project is Isoloop. Its packages are published under the `@isoloop/*` npm scope, and the CLI as the unscoped `isoloop`.

events.why: An isolated event loop per unit is what the runtime gives, visual or headless, and the name was free on npm, as an npm scope and as a GitHub org.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: The packages aren't published under the working name Federa.

events.why: Why not keep Federa? The `@federa` npm scope belongs to another maintainer, so `@federa/host` couldn't be published and npm searches would mix us with an unrelated project.

statement: System topics are named `isoloop.*`, for example `isoloop.route.v1`, and the host's surface element is `<iso-surface>`.

events.why: One prefix per kind of name, taken from the project's name.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Every `@isoloop/*` package and the `isoloop` CLI share one version, through one Changesets `fixed` group.

events.why: `runtime` and `host` must always speak the same render format, so they're released together.
The CLI joins the group, so one number names a build across every package.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Each app in `isoloop/web` (`plant-v*`, `markets-v*`, `processor-v*`, `site-v*`) has its own version, apart from the library's, and the maintainer pushes its tags.

events.why: The apps deploy on their own schedule, so tying them to the library's version would say nothing.
In force from the ADR's PR.

statement: The host-to-worker protocol (`PROTOCOL { v, min }`) may change in any release.

events.why: Both ends ship in one build, so no released version ever talks to another.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Previews are `x.y.z-next.N` versions under npm `next`, made in Changesets pre mode `next`. Releases are plain `x.y.z` under `latest`.

events.why: `0.0.0-next.<sha>` didn't sort by time and led to no release.
Changesets went into pre mode `next`, with the version step and the changeset check.

statement: In pre mode a version PR moves only the `-next.N` counter, whatever the changesets' bump types.

events.why: That's how Changesets pre mode counts, so previews of one minor stay in order.
Changesets went into pre mode `next`.

statement: On 0.x a minor may contain anything: breaking changes, and additions to the isolate seam (`IsolateContext`, `defineIsolate`, the DOM subset, the adapter hooks).

events.why: The isolate check compares only `major.minor`, so a seam member added in a patch would pass the check on an older host and then fail.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: On 0.x a patch holds fixes plus compatible additions outside the isolate seam: the host API, `KernelConfig` and new packages.

events.why: Host-side additions don't need the isolate check, so they needn't wait for a minor.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: From 1.0 the versions are plain semver: a major breaks, a minor adds, the isolate seam included, and a patch fixes.

events.why: From 1.0 the isolate check compares majors, so a minor may add to the seam.

statement: An `@experimental` API may change or be removed in any minor, before and after 1.0.

events.why: Tying 1.0 to every new API settling would hold 1.0 back on a browser shipping WebMCP and on the balancer's design.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Each `@experimental` API is marked `@experimental` in its TSDoc, and a change to it is called out in the changelog.

events.why: A promise that may change in any minor has to be visible where people read the API.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: An API leaves `@experimental` through a decision recorded in its ADR. From then on it follows the minor and patch rules.

events.why: Leaving experimental is a promise to users, so it's decided on the record.
In force from the ADR's PR.

statement: A patch to the current release during a preview cycle comes from a `release/0.x` branch, cut from the latest `v0.x.y` tag only when a fix is needed.

events.why: Pre mode applies to the whole repo, so `main` can't release a patch while it previews the next minor.
`release.yml` releases from `release/0.1` as well as `main`, for 0.1.1.

statement: A fix goes to `main` first. Its backport to the release branch is its own PR, with its own regression test.

events.why: A fix that skips `main` comes back as a regression in the next minor.
In force from the amendment's PR.

statement: Only a small, reviewable backport goes to a release branch. A larger fix ships in the next minor, brought forward if it's urgent.

events.why: Backports are made by hand, and a large one is a second change nobody tested on `main`.
In force from the amendment's PR.

statement: A release branch can stage only once it's admitted: added to the `npm` environment by its exact name, with a ruleset of its own. `release.yml` accepts `main` and that branch by exact name.

events.why: A pattern such as `release/*` would also match version-PR branches, which no ruleset protects.
`RELEASE_BRANCHES` lists `main` and `release/0.1`.

statement: One release branch exists at a time. It's deleted when the next minor takes `latest`, keeps its tags, and is never merged back into `main`.

events.why: Only the latest release is supported, so an older line needs no branch.
In force from the amendment's PR.

statement: No patch is released for an older line. `release.yml` refuses a version that would move `latest` or `next` back.

events.why: Once 0.2.0 is `latest`, a 0.1.x must not take that dist-tag back.
The stage run checks each package's current dist-tags before it stages.

statement: There's no standing `release/0.x` branch for every minor.

events.why: Why not keep a branch per minor? It costs a ruleset, CI, a Changesets state and hand cherry-picks every week, for a line users are told to leave.

statement: Every published version has an annotated tag `v<version>` on the commit it was built from, made by the `finish` run after the publish. Pushing a tag starts nothing.

events.why: One tag per version answers which commit a build came from.
The tags ruleset forbids moving a tag, so a tag made before a rejected stage would stay on the wrong commit.
events.prev: The Prerelease workflow tagged previews after publishing, and a release tag pushed by the maintainer started the release.

events.why: Staged releases from `release.yml`, with `finish` making the tag.

statement: A release isn't started by pushing its tag.

events.why: Why not tag first and let the tag start the release? A tag can't be moved or deleted, so a rejected stage would leave the version's tag on the wrong commit for good.

statement: Each release from 0.1.0 on gets a GitHub Release, made by `finish`; previews get none. Its text is `.github/releases/<version>.md` where that file exists, and the changelog sections otherwise.

events.why: Previews are for this project and `isoloop/web`, and their tag and changelogs are enough.
0.1.0's changelogs would repeat every preview's entries, so a release can carry its own text.
events.prev: Each release from 0.1.0 on gets a GitHub Release; previews get none.

events.why: `finish` makes the Release.

statement: Every version, preview or release, is published by one workflow, `release.yml`. It's started by hand, it's a dry run unless told otherwise, and the npm dist-tag comes from the version.

events.why: One path to audit, and previews rehearse the path a release takes.
Staged releases from `release.yml`.

statement: A version is staged by `release.yml`, then the maintainer approves each of the 13 packages on npmjs.com with 2FA, then a `finish` run checks every package's version, dist-tag and provenance before it tags.

events.why: A publish then needs the maintainer's 2FA, which an agent or a job holding GitHub credentials doesn't have.
Staged releases from `release.yml`.

statement: The maintainer approves the staged packages in dependency order: protocol, codec, dom and vite; then bus and runtime; then host, react and preact; then balancer, devtools, webmcp and the `isoloop` CLI. None is approved until all 13 are staged.

events.why: Each approval moves a dist-tag at once, so this order keeps what's on npm installable at every step.
`APPROVAL_ORDER` holds the order, and the stage summary follows it.

statement: Each package trusts only `release.yml` in the `npm` environment, allowed to stage and not to publish or change dist-tags. Tokens are disallowed, and there's no fallback publish.

events.why: npm accepts a publish that matches any one trust entry, so the gate holds only if it's the only way in.
Staged releases from `release.yml`.

statement: Packages aren't published directly from a GitHub environment, for releases or previews.

events.why: Why not publish from a protected environment and skip the approvals? Whoever holds the maintainer's GitHub credentials, as agents do, can change the environment and publish.

statement: Staged packages are approved in the browser, not with the npm CLI.

events.why: Why not approve 13 packages faster from the CLI? Agents share that shell's npm session, and npm can skip 2FA for 5 minutes after a prompt.

statement: GitHub Pages isn't part of a release. It serves a redirect to isoloop.dev, and `pages.yml` is run by hand when that changes.

events.why: The redirect doesn't change with a release, and the `github-pages` environment refuses deploys from tags.
Staged releases from `release.yml`, with no Pages step.

statement: The changeset check fails a changeset that asks for a `major` bump while the version is below 1.0.0, unless the PR has the `release-1.0` label.

events.why: On 0.x a breaking change is a minor, so a major is a mistake until 1.0's previews start.
Changeset guards for majors and version PRs.

statement: A PR whose diff only consumes changesets passes the changeset check without the `no-changeset` label. The check reads the diff, not the branch name.

events.why: A version PR has no changeset of its own by design.
Changeset guards for majors and version PRs.

statement: `release.yml` stages only when every package has the same version: a `-next.N` in pre mode, or a plain `x.y.z` out of it.

events.why: Packages in one fixed group must never reach npm at different versions.
Releases go through the same workflow as previews, so the check covers both.
events.prev: The preview workflow stages only when every package has the same `-next.N` version.

events.why: Staged releases from `release.yml`.

statement: Every `0.0.0*` version of each `@isoloop/*` package is deprecated on npm, not unpublished.

events.why: Unpublishing would break old lockfiles, and npm limits it anyway.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Only the version on npm `latest` is supported. `next` previews are never supported.

events.why: On 0.x a minor may break anything, so a second supported line would mean backports to code users were told to leave.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: A security bug in an unsupported version is fixed in `latest` and published as a GitHub security advisory that names the affected range and the fixed version.

events.why: Users of an old line still need to learn they're affected and where the fix is.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: A version range is deprecated on npm, with the message "Upgrade to latest", only for a known security or data-loss bug.

events.why: Deprecating every superseded minor would warn on every install for no known risk.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: The previous minor gets no support window on 0.x.

events.why: Why not support the previous minor for a while? On 0.x a minor may break anything. The question comes back at 1.0.

statement: Each minor's changesets name its breaking changes and how to migrate. The steward checks it.

events.why: Users who must upgrade to stay supported need to know what breaks.
In force from the amendment's PR.

statement: A breaking change to a stable API ships with a codemod that migrates it, in the same release, or it doesn't ship. Stable means every export the API check compares, except `@internal` ones.

events.why: Moving the web apps to 0.1.0 meant migrating each API change by hand.
`isoloop migrate`, the codemod gate and the parser interface.

statement: A changeset whose summary starts with `breaking:` fails the changeset check unless the PR adds codemod fixtures under `packages/cli/src/migrate/<version>/fixtures/`.

events.why: The rule holds only if CI holds a breaking change to it.
`isoloop migrate`, the codemod gate and the parser interface.

statement: `npx isoloop migrate` reads the installed `@isoloop/*` version and applies each codemod up to the latest; `npx isoloop migrate 0.2` names the target. It's a dry run that prints the diff unless given `--write`.

events.why: Users get each breaking change's migration from one command, in order.
`isoloop migrate`, the codemod gate and the parser interface.

statement: A behaviour change with no syntax to rewrite gets an `// isoloop-migrate:` comment where the code uses it, and a migration section in the guide.

events.why: A codemod can't rewrite behaviour, but it can point at every place that depends on it.
`isoloop migrate`, the codemod gate and the parser interface.

statement: Codemods parse TypeScript and JSX with `oxc-parser`, behind Isoloop's own `parse` and `edit` interface with conformance tests, and rewrite by text edits so the user's formatting is kept.

events.why: It comes from the same project as the repo's oxlint and oxfmt, needs no printer, and can be swapped for TypeScript 7's own API once that's stable.
`isoloop migrate`, the codemod gate and the parser interface.

statement: A change to an `@experimental` API gets a codemod when the change is mechanical, and a migration note otherwise.

events.why: Experimental APIs may change in any minor, but a mechanical rewrite still costs users nothing.
In force from the amendment's PR.

statement: `isoloop/web`'s plant-bench runs the codemods on every run branch that needs them, and a codemod that fails there blocks the release.

events.why: Fixtures prove a codemod on small cases; real apps prove it on code nobody wrote for it.
